name: Eurocommunism
summary: Eurocommunism was the 1970s current of the Italian and Spanish communist parties (with the French party only partly) that sought socialism through democracy and pluralism, not through a dictatorship of the proletariat. Berlinguer called democracy a historically universal value and, with Carrillo, pledged a plurality of parties, universal suffrage, a full list of civil liberties and democratic alternation, in a lay, non-ideological state. They claimed independence from Moscow, kept democratic centralism inside their own parties, and sought broad alliances including Catholics. Carrillo argued that the capitalist state could be democratised from within, with public and private property side by side for a long period.
scope: The Eurocommunist line of the PCI under Enrico Berlinguer and the PCE under Santiago Carrillo, c. 1973-1982: Berlinguer's Moscow speech of 1977, the Livorno (1975), Paris (1975) and Madrid (1977) joint declarations, and Carrillo's Eurocommunism and the State. The PCF's partial turn (1976-78), Marxism-Leninism and later social-democratic successors are excluded, and general anti-fascism, labour-movement values and Soviet-bloc positions are not borrowed.

democracy-best.rationale: Berlinguer's Moscow speech calls democracy a historically universal value on which a socialist society is to be founded, and the Madrid communiqué commits the parties to universal suffrage and the democratic alternation of majorities, which accepts what voters decide.

one-party-rule.rationale: The Livorno and Paris joint declarations and the Madrid communiqué call for a plurality of parties, the right of opposition parties to exist and democratic alternation, and Berlinguer's speech names several parties and a non-ideological state; Carrillo explicitly gave up the one-party state.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Carrillo rejected the dictatorship of the proletariat as a notion belonging to a time when the working class was a minority; US-army and scholarly accounts report that the PCI, PCE and PCF all dropped the concept.

workers-councils.rationale: Carrillo renounced the classic workers' and peasants' state built on a new plan and sought to democratise the existing parliamentary state, and the parties pledge universal suffrage and alternation, which leave no room for councils replacing parliaments.

direct-action.rationale: The parties pursue socialism through a democratic advance in peace and liberty by winning majorities and alliances, with respect for universal suffrage, not through direct action in place of elections and parliaments.

party-commands-army.rationale: A non-ideological state, a plurality of parties and democratic alternation (Berlinguer 1977, Madrid 1977) rule out a ruling party commanding the army; Carrillo wanted a national army loyal to the state.

party-controls-media.rationale: The Madrid communiqué lists freedom of thought, speech and press and the freedom of different currents of opinion among the liberties to be guaranteed under socialism.

total-state.rationale: Berlinguer's Moscow speech calls for a non-ideological state and pluralism in social, cultural and ideal life, and Madrid guarantees cultural freedom, so the state may not direct every area of life.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: The parties hold that socialism must be built in democracy and liberty and must guarantee all personal and collective liberties, with no exception for development.

organic-representation.rationale: Their programme rests on a plurality of political parties, universal suffrage and democratic alternation of majorities, so representation through parties is central, not replaced.

clerical-rule.rationale: The joint declarations call for the lay nature of the state and Berlinguer for a non-ideological state, which excludes rule by senior clergy.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: A lay, non-ideological state with religious freedom (joint declarations, Berlinguer 1977) is incompatible with laws grounded in scripture.

sacred-ruler.rationale: The lay nature of the state in the joint declarations excludes a head of state treated as sacred or of divine descent.

separate-church-state.rationale: The joint declarations call for the lay nature of the state and Berlinguer for a non-ideological state; Berlinguer also sought an accommodation with Catholics, so the separation is not hostile.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: The Madrid communiqué lists cultural freedom and the freedom of philosophical, cultural and artistic currents among the liberties to be guaranteed.

public-ownership.rationale: Carrillo lists nationalisation of key sectors of the economy among the structural reforms that change the nature of the state, alongside a long coexistence of public and private property.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Carrillo's structural reforms include self-management in enterprises and direct democracy, though he gives no detail on how large companies are governed.

unions-good.rationale: The Madrid communiqué commits the parties to union freedom, union independence and the right to strike as liberties of the society they want.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Carrillo holds that the state continues to be an instrument of class domination, while arguing that it can be democratised from within without being smashed.

socialism-one-country.rationale: Carrillo argues that full socialism cannot be built in one country unless it also triumphs in a series of advanced countries, and ties Soviet distortions to capitalist encirclement.

soviet-state-capitalist.rationale: Carrillo calls the Soviet state not a bourgeois state but an intermediate one short of a workers' democracy, and the PCI never questioned its socialist character, so neither strand calls it state capitalism.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: The PCI and PCE favoured a stronger, supranational Europe as a factor of stability and a counterweight to the superpowers, and the PCI ended its opposition to integration; the PCF opposed it and is outside this profile's core.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Berlinguer says the PCI does not ask for Italy to leave NATO and feels safer inside it, whereas the PCE treated Spain's membership differently, so the two parties are split on permanent alliances.

vanguard-party.rationale: Carrillo calls the PCE a vanguard in so far as it embodies a creative Marxist attitude but no longer the only representative of the working class and with no monopoly of power; democratic centralism stayed in all three parties.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: The PCI, PCE and PCF kept democratic centralism; Berlinguer reaffirmed it in 1983 as the party's form of internal life.

people-in-arms.rationale: Carrillo called for a national army capable of defence and a left government that wins the professional soldiers to the new state, which keeps a professional army.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: Carrillo's strategy builds a hegemonic bloc of labour and culture and democratises the state without destroying it by force, which is opposed to a small armed group creating revolution.

notes: Themes searched: government (parties, alternation, suffrage, judiciary, army, the constitutional road), liberty (the Madrid list of freedoms, unions), economy (planning, private enterprise, austerity, mixed property), society (lay state, Church, divorce and abortion, women, culture), world (NATO, EEC, USSR and Czechoslovakia, coexistence, arms, Third World), culture, ecology, technology. Texts read: Berlinguer's Chile reflections (1973), 14th Congress report and resolution (1975), Casalegno (1976), Pansa (1976), Berlin (1976), Eliseo austerity speech (1977), Moscow speech (1977), and the Madrid communique (1977). Carrillo's Eurocommunism and the State is known only through Harman's and Adant's quotations (the Internet Archive scans are lending-only or unreachable), the PCE's 1975 Manifiesto-Programa, the 9th Congress theses and the Livorno and Paris declarations were not found as full text, and the 15th PCI Congress report was not found. Positions held only by the PCI (abortion and divorce law, taxes, tax evasion, health, consumerism, proportional representation, anti-fascism as a constitutional value, banning neo-fascist groups) are null because PCE sources were not found to share them. The PCF is outside the core (it differed on NATO, the deterrent and the EEC), the PCI and PCE split on NATO membership, and the sources record little on ecology or technology.
